slots.practicalActivity: Write a short paragraph describing a real time you (or a project you've seen) lost work or got confused tracking changes without version control — emailing files back and forth, overwriting a colleague's edit, or renaming files '_final_v2'. Then confirm Git is installed on your machine by running git --version in a terminal; if it isn't, install it now.
slots.deliverable: A short written paragraph describing a real version-control pain point, plus a terminal screenshot of a working git --version output.

slots.practicalActivity: Set your Git identity with git config --global user.name "Your Name" and git config --global user.email "you@example.com", then create a new scratch folder and run git init inside it. Confirm the hidden .git folder exists, and run git status to see the clean, empty-repository state.
slots.deliverable: A real local Git repository created with git init, with global user.name/user.email configured and confirmed via git config --list.

slots.practicalActivity: In your scratch repository, create 3 files. Stage only 2 of them with git add, run git status to confirm the third is still untracked, commit the staged 2 with a specific, descriptive message (not 'update'), then stage and commit the third file separately with its own clear message. Run git log to see both commits.
slots.deliverable: A repository with 2 separate, clearly-messaged commits built from deliberately split staging, confirmed with a git log showing both.

slots.practicalActivity: From main, create a new branch feature/readme with git branch or git switch -c, switch to it, edit or create a file, and commit the change on that branch. Run git branch to list all branches and confirm which one is currently checked out, then switch back to main and confirm the file change is not there.
slots.deliverable: A new feature branch with its own commit, plus git branch output confirming both branches exist and the change is isolated to the feature branch.

slots.practicalActivity: Create two separate branches off main, each adding a different new file with its own commit. Merge the first branch into main with git merge (producing a merge commit), then rebase the second branch onto main with git rebase main before merging it. Run git log --graph --oneline --all on the final result and compare the two different shapes it shows for the merge vs. the rebase path.
slots.deliverable: A git log --graph output showing one branch integrated via a true merge commit and a second integrated via rebase, with a one-sentence note on the visible difference in history shape.

slots.practicalActivity: Create two branches off main that each edit the exact same line of the same file differently, commit both, then attempt to merge one into the other to deliberately trigger a real conflict. Open the file, find the <<<<<<< / ======= / >>>>>>> conflict markers, manually resolve them to the content you want, then git add the resolved file and complete the merge with git commit.
slots.deliverable: A real, deliberately-triggered merge conflict, hand-resolved by editing the conflict markers directly, staged, and completed with a final merge commit.

slots.practicalActivity: Create a real new repository on GitHub.com (public or private, your choice). In your local scratch repository, add it as a remote with git remote add origin <url>, then confirm it's attached correctly by running git remote -v.
slots.deliverable: A real repository created on GitHub.com, linked to your local repository as 'origin', confirmed with git remote -v output.

slots.practicalActivity: Push your local commits to GitHub with git push -u origin main, then confirm they appear on GitHub.com. Edit a file directly in GitHub's web editor and commit it there, then run git fetch locally and inspect what changed (without merging yet) before running git pull to actually bring the remote change down.
slots.deliverable: Local commits successfully pushed to a real GitHub repo, plus a remote-made change pulled back down locally, with git fetch run and inspected separately from git pull.

slots.practicalActivity: Create a new feature branch, make a real change, push it to GitHub, and open a real pull request comparing it against main with a clear title and a description explaining what changed and why. Walk through its Conversation, Commits, Checks, and Files changed tabs and note what each one shows for your specific PR.
slots.deliverable: A real, open pull request on your GitHub repository with a clear title/description, plus written notes on what each of its four tabs showed for this specific PR.

slots.practicalActivity: On the pull request's Files changed tab, leave a real inline review comment on a specific line (self-review is fine if working solo), request changes via GitHub's review feature, then push a follow-up commit to the same branch addressing that comment and mark the conversation as resolved.
slots.deliverable: A real review comment left on a specific line of a pull request's diff, a follow-up commit addressing it, and that conversation thread marked resolved.

slots.practicalActivity: Open 3 real GitHub Issues on your repository describing small, specific tasks. Create a Project board with To Do / In Progress / Done columns and place all 3 issues on it, moving at least one across columns. Reference and auto-close one issue from a commit or pull request description using a closing keyword like 'Closes #1'.
slots.deliverable: 3 real GitHub Issues organized on a Project board with at least one moved across columns, and one issue auto-closed via a commit or PR closing keyword.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a short markdown note sketching how your repository would be organized under Git Flow (main/develop/feature/release branches) versus Trunk-Based Development (short-lived branches merged directly into main). Then actually pick one of the two models and create the real branch structure it requires in your repository (e.g. a develop branch, or one short-lived feature branch merged same-day).
slots.deliverable: A written comparison of Git Flow vs. Trunk-Based branching for your specific repository, plus the real branch structure for whichever model you chose, created in the repo.

slots.practicalActivity: Find a small, actively-maintained public open-source repository on GitHub and fork it into your own account. Clone your fork locally, create a branch, make one small, genuinely useful change (a typo fix, a doc clarification), push it to your fork, and open a real pull request back to the upstream project — or, if the project isn't a good fit for an unsolicited PR, stop after pushing to your fork and explain in one sentence why you didn't submit it upstream.
slots.deliverable: A real fork of a public repository with a branch, a committed and pushed change, and either a real pull request opened to the upstream project or a written one-sentence reason it was withheld.

slots.practicalActivity: Pick a file in your repository with several commits across it and run git blame on it to see which commit last touched each line. Then run git log -p --follow on a file you've renamed at some point (rename one now if you haven't) to confirm Git still traces its full history through the rename.
slots.deliverable: Real git blame output identifying the commit behind specific lines of a file, plus git log -p --follow output tracing a file's history across a rename.

slots.practicalActivity: Create a real annotated tag on your repository's main branch with git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "First tagged version", push it with git push origin v1.0.0, then go to GitHub.com and create an actual Release from that tag with a short set of release notes describing what's in it.
slots.deliverable: A real annotated Git tag pushed to GitHub, with a corresponding GitHub Release created from it containing written release notes.

slots.practicalActivity: Add a .gitignore file to your repository excluding at least 3 realistic patterns relevant to your project (e.g. __pycache__/, .env, *.log, node_modules/). Create one of those excluded files and confirm git status no longer shows it. If a similar junk file was already committed before the .gitignore existed, use git rm --cached on it to untrack it without deleting it from disk.
slots.deliverable: A real .gitignore file excluding at least 3 patterns, with a demonstrated file that git status correctly ignores, and (if applicable) one previously-tracked file untracked via git rm --cached.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending lab for Collaborative Workflows: on your real repository, ship one small feature end to end the professional way — create a branch under the strategy you chose earlier, commit the work, merge it to main, tag the resulting release, and confirm your .gitignore is correctly keeping build artifacts or secrets out of the commit.
slots.deliverable: One real feature shipped end-to-end on your repository: a branch, a merge to main, a pushed tag/release for it, and confirmation that .gitignore kept the commit clean.

slots.practicalActivity: Pick a real, actively-maintained public GitHub repository (one you use or admire) and open its .github/workflows/ folder. Read one workflow file to determine whether the project practices Continuous Integration, Continuous Delivery, or Continuous Deployment, based on what triggers its steps. Write two sentences arguing which of Delivery or Deployment you'd choose for your own repository, and why.
slots.deliverable: A short written determination of which CI/CD stage a real public project's workflow file implements, plus a 2-sentence argument for Delivery vs. Deployment on your own project.

slots.practicalActivity: Add a real .github/workflows/ci.yml file to your repository that triggers on every push, checks out the code, and runs at least one simple command (even just echo "CI ran" or printing the file listing). Push it, then watch it actually execute and go green in your repository's Actions tab.
slots.deliverable: A real .github/workflows/ci.yml committed and pushed to your repository, with at least one successful green run visible in the GitHub Actions tab.

slots.practicalActivity: Add a real, simple test file to your repository (e.g. a one-function pytest test, or an equivalent for whatever language your repo uses). Extend ci.yml to set up the language runtime, install dependencies, and actually run the test suite on every push and pull request, confirming a real green check appears on your next PR.
slots.deliverable: A real test file added to the repository, with ci.yml extended to install dependencies and run it automatically, shown passing as a real check on a pull request.

slots.practicalActivity: Add a second job to ci.yml that only runs when a push lands on main (using an if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' condition), simulating a deploy step (even just echoing "deploying to production" or copying a build artifact). Push a change on a feature branch first to confirm the deploy job does not run, then merge to main and confirm it does.
slots.deliverable: A conditional deploy job in ci.yml that is proven, by two real pushes, to skip on a feature branch and run only after a merge to main.

lessons.title: Capstone: A Project With a Real GitHub Workflow

slots.practicalActivity: Build one small real project repository from scratch that applies everything from this course: meaningful init/add/commit history, a feature branch merged via a real pull request with a code-review pass, at least one Issue tracked on a Project board, a pushed tag with a GitHub Release, a working .gitignore, and a working GitHub Actions CI workflow that runs tests on every push.
slots.deliverable: One complete capstone repository on GitHub exhibiting real commit history, a merged PR with review, an issue tracked on a project board, a tagged release, a working .gitignore, and a green CI workflow.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a clear top-level README.md for the capstone repository describing what the project does, how its branching/PR/CI workflow is organized, and how to run it. Write 3-4 interview-ready sentences describing the Git/GitHub workflow skills this repository demonstrates, ready to say out loud in a real interview.
slots.deliverable: A polished README.md on the capstone repository, plus a short written interview pitch (3-4 sentences) describing the demonstrated Git/GitHub workflow skills.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After this course, a student can independently run a real Git and GitHub workflow — branching, merging, resolving conflicts, opening and reviewing pull requests, tagging releases, and running tests automatically via GitHub Actions CI — and has a live, documented capstone repository on GitHub to show for it.
